newsitem.title: USA: U.S. safety panel calls for B-737 changes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. safety panel calls for B-737 changes.

text.p: U.S. safety officials on Wednesday recommended immediate sweeping changes in the "rudder and yaw" control systems of the widely used Boeing 737 airliner to try to avoid sudden and uncontrolled rolls.

Included in the National Transportation Safety Board's recommendations to the Federal Aviation Administration were rudder design changes by Boeing and new training for pilots on how to combat such uncommanded movements.
The board's recommendations followed a series of still unexplained 737 crashes, including one of a USAir plane near Pittsburgh in September 1994 in which all 132 people on board were killed.
Investigators believe the crashes were triggered by sharp sudden rolls before the aircraft came in to land.
Officials said the recommended changes might not get to the cause of the accidents but would make 737s safer.
After its own review of the 737, the FAA last August pronounced it safe. But it proposed a series of changes to improve the planes' safety.
About 2,600 737s are flown by airlines worldwide.

The board recommended the FAA require Boeing to make long-term design changes to preclude a loss of control from a rudder "hard-over" -- an extreme rudder shift that could throw the plane into a sharp roll.
It also recommended a redesign of the plane's rudder damper system to prevent yaws -- the movement of the nose from side to side -- so the rudder would not move into an extreme roll-causing position.
In addition, the board called for an indicator system, not now in the cockpit, to show the pilot the position and movement of the rudder.
The board stressed the need for additional training procedures by Boeing and operators of 737s to require crews to disengage the yaw damper in case of an uncontrolled roll.

It said Boeing should develop procedures for 737 pilots to deal effectively with a sudden uncommanded rudder movement and then 737 operators to give the necessary training to pilots on how to get out ot an uncontrolled roll.
The FAA and Boeing had no immediate comment on the board's recommendations.
